source.version: Undated English author manuscript labeled Academic Paper for the 28th Annual Meeting of the China Association for Science and Technology. PDF p. 1 states that it is an author-proofread translation of a Chinese original and that the Chinese version prevails. The supplied citation record identifies this saved file as PsyArXiv v1, DOI 10.31234/osf.io/7x2v3_v1; the saved document itself prints no version date. This extraction uses the supplied manuscript, not the later publisher PDF identified by the citation record.
source.supplement_used: Same PDF: Appendix, PDF pp. 39–41 (Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Tables 1–2); Appendix 1: Task Instructions, PDF pp. 42–44.

studies.label: Laboratory collaboration experiment: alternative uses and product improvement

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 1, Abstract; arm counts: PDF p. 15, Table 1; task-specific analyzed counts: PDF p. 8, section 2.1
counts_source.quote: This study employed a between-subjects experimental design with a sample of 169 university students, who were randomly assigned to either the human−human collaboration or human−AI collaboration groups.

arms.name: Human in HAI
arms.description: Human collaborates with GPT–5–mini through a custom chat interface, alternating one idea per turn, human first. The AI receives a task-specific prompt. Randomized human count is printed in Table 1 as 'HAI (55)' (PDF p. 15); the unique analyzed human count across both tasks is not printed.

arms.name: Human in HH
arms.description: Human collaborates with another randomly assigned human, alternating ideas through the same interface. The partners draw lots for first speaker and then work in separate rooms. Randomized human count is printed in Table 1 as 'HH (114)' (PDF p. 15); the unique analyzed human count across both tasks is not printed.

studies.task: The same university students brainstormed unusual uses for a rubber band (AUT; divergent_test) and creative chair improvements (PIT; idea_generation), in random task order with an assigned human or AI partner.

ai_tool.name: GPT–5–mini
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 9, section 2.2: names the model and dates of API use but does not state its release year.

preregistration.where: No preregistration is stated in the manuscript or appendices. PDF p. 9, section 2.2 calls novelty, usefulness, flexibility, and fluency primary outcomes without identifying a preregistration.

studies.shared_sample: No other paper is stated to reuse these participants. AUT and PIT use the same recruited sample with task-specific exclusions; they are not independent studies (PDF p. 9, section 2.1; PDF p. 10, section 2.3).

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique: two graduate students with creativity research backgrounds independently rated ideas on a seven-point scale, blind to condition, identity, and hypotheses. Ratings were averaged across raters and across each individual's ideas (PDF p. 13, section 2.5).

sources.locator: PDF p. 39, Supplementary Figure 1, panels A–B and caption, definition
sources.quote: For each current idea produced by a given role, forward flow was calculated as the mean semantic distance between that idea and all preceding valid ideas from the same group in the same task.

sources.locator: PDF p. 39, Supplementary Figure 1, caption, direction
sources.quote: A higher score indicates a weaker semantic relationship with preceding ideas and a larger semantic shift.

estimates.notes: Higher values indicate a larger semantic shift away from earlier ideas within the same dyad, rather than diversity across independent participants. The plotted uncertainty has an unspecified unit and error-bar definition, so se_basis is unclear. The task's general valid human count is not substituted for an unreported forward-flow analysis count.

open_items: The unique analyzed human sample across both tasks and unique arm totals are not printed; task-specific valid human totals cannot be added because the tasks share participants (PDF pp. 8–10).

Task-specific human counts per arm are not explicitly printed as people. The between-condition tables label dyads; no dyad-to-person conversion, exclusion subtraction, or derivation from degrees of freedom was performed.
Tables 2 and 4 do not define their parenthetical dispersion values as SD or SE. Their values are preserved verbatim in row quotes, but the SD and SE fields are null (PDF pp. 17 and 21).

Human-only arm means, SDs, SEs, mean differences, and confidence intervals are not tabulated. Reported d values lack a stated standardizer and uncertainty; they are transcribed without treating them as a verified participant-SD effect (PDF pp. 17–18 and 22).
The weighting of individual or idea-level novelty and usefulness scores into whole-dyad means is not specified (PDF p. 13, section 2.5; PDF pp. 17 and 21, Tables 2 and 4).

Forward flow lacks the semantic model, distance algorithm, role-mean aggregation rule, analysis unit and counts, test specification, error-bar definition, and numerical summaries. All figure-only statistics remain null (PDF p. 39).

The exact random-effects and residual specifications for the unadjusted role comparisons are not separately detailed. Individual aggregation is stated; dyad random intercepts are explicitly described in the APIM methods (PDF pp. 13–15).
PIT delayed perspective taking is described as nonsignificant in the human-only results and marginally significant in the discussion; no exact pairwise p value is supplied (PDF pp. 22 and 29).
The model release year is not stated. The manuscript dates API use, which is not treated as a verified release year (PDF p. 9).
The citation record identifies a later journal version. Numerical correspondence between that version and the supplied manuscript is not established by this extraction; no versions were mixed.
notes: The complete markdown was read from start to end, including references and appendices. Every cited PDF page was extracted with pymupdf. PDF and printed page numbers agree. Tables 2 and 4 were confirmed from PDF text; find_tables returned no tables on those pages. No effect sizes, uncertainty measures, arm counts, or figure values were computed. Study counts are people: Table 1 prints 'HAI (55)' and 'HH (114)' (PDF p. 15), and section 2.1 prints valid task totals of 155 for AUT and 164 for PIT (PDF p. 8). In contrast, Table 2 headers are 'HAI (49)' and 'HH (53)' dyads (PDF p. 17), and Table 4 headers are 'HAI (54)' and 'HH (55)' dyads (PDF p. 21); these are retained here as dyad-count metadata and are not placed in people-count fields. Random task order is not crossover assignment to assistance: each person kept the same collaboration condition. Whole-dyad contrasts include human participation and therefore are retained separately from human-only contrasts, with pair-based uncertainty. Category convergence and forward flow concern ongoing interaction within a dyad and are coded other/with_ai, not across_people diversity. No eligible after_ai outcome is reported. Preregistration is not stated; the paper's description of primary performance outcomes is not treated as evidence of preregistration. Extraction date: 2026-10-11.
